title: A Three-Question Checklist for Building Stronger Relationships through Moments of Genuine Connection ments-of-genuine-connection
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. builds on his "moments of genuine connection" (MGC) framework by introducing a self-diagnostic tool drawn from Kate Murphy's book You're Not Listening. He first clarifies that consistently attempting MGCs — not guaranteeing their success — is what makes the practice effective, breaking the definition into five components: consistency, attempting, genuineness, connection, and inclusion of all students. He then presents Murphy's three post-conversation questions (what did I learn about the person, what were they most concerned about, how did they feel) as a way to score how well a teacher is actually listening during MGC attempts, citing Uri Hasson's neuroscience research on listener-speaker brain synchronization as evidence that listening skill is trainable. The piece closes with a six-step practice protocol for using a printable checklist over five days to diagnose and improve one's listening.
points: MGC effectiveness comes from consistent attempts across all students, not from guaranteeing every interaction lands — a distinction Stuart says "grounds us in our finitude."
Murphy's three questions (what did I learn, what were they concerned about, how did they feel) function as a self-diagnostic score for listening quality during MGC attempts.
Uri Hasson's fMRI research on brain-wave synchronization between speaker and listener is cited as evidence that "connection" during listening is a measurable, trainable phenomenon.
The six-step practice protocol (scoring yourself over five consecutive days using the checklist) gives teachers a concrete way to track improvement in listening skill over time.
quotes: After a moment of genuine connection, we want students to feel valued, known, or respected. This produces all kinds of benefits, like enhancing belonging, reducing stereotype threat, and strengthening our teacher credibility.

The effectiveness of tracking MGCs doesn't come from them producing perfect results each time we attempt them. Rather, the effectiveness comes from consistently attempting to genuinely connect with all students.

In one experiment, subjects listened to a conversation partner describe a scene from the BBC television series Sherlock. During the recollection, the speaker's brain waves looked much the same as when the speaker was actually watching the show.
If we can't answer those three questions, then chances are the person we were speaking with didn't feel very listened to.
Was I really listening to my students today, or was I going through the motions? If we can't answer these three questions, Murphy argues, it's unlikely that our students felt fully listened to.
Like shooting a basket or throwing a trident (why not?), MGCs are something we can get better at.
